newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto stocks follow Wall Street lower.
newsitem.headline: Toronto stocks follow Wall Street lower.

text.p: Toronto's key stock index lost 1.1 percent on Monday as Wall Street sold off sharply after comments by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan may sell U.S. government securities.

The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index dropped 73.72 points to 6437.71. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell almost 2.5 percent or 192 points to 7604, its second largest single-day point drop ever, trailing only Black Monday's 508-point crash on October 19, 1987.
Portfolio consultant Ron Meisels added that profit-takers rushed in on the heels of Friday's triple-witching volatility.
"This comes on the Monday following a triple-witching exploration, which, if the market is up previous to that, has often created significant sell-offs," Meisels said.
Toronto trading was modest at 80.3 million shares worth C$1.47 billion ($1.01 billion).

Hashimoto said in a New York speech that "I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off treasury bills and switch our funds to gold."
Almost all of Toronto's 14 sub-indexes tumbled except for real estate and banks. Base metals, golds and consumer products led the retreat.
Losing issues outnumbered gainers 600 to 394, and 274 finished flat.
Influential miner Barrick Gold Corp. topped Toronto actives, falling 1.15 to 30.70 on 3.7 million shares.
Telecommunications firms led net losing issues. Northern Telecom Ltd. fell 5 to 119.75, while Newbridge Networks Corp. fell 2.30 to 59.50.

Bombardier Inc.'s class B shares ended 0.30 higher at 31.45. The transportation company's de Havilland unit reached a tentative labor contract with unionized workers on Monday, narrowly averting a strike, the union said.
